This paper introduces a method for 3D instrument guidance tailored to retinal surgery, a field where high precision is critical. Our approach utilizes a camera-equipped microscope to capture the surgical environment, with a specific focus on guiding instruments used in vitreoretinal procedures. We developed a framework to determine the 3D positions of these tools by leveraging a technique known as "spotlight tracking," which involves identifying the intersection of two light rays generated by a spotlight on the microscope's optical assembly. This system was validated through experiments using a physical setup that simulated a real surgical environment.

The F-polynomials, originally defined by Fomin and Zelevinsky within the framework of the geometric combinatorics of cluster algebras, are central to understanding the dual nature of these cluster algebras. This paper presents a recursive method for calculating F-polynomials in the cluster algebra of a marked surface with punctures and boundary components. This approach is derived from the combinatorics of the F-polynomials in the associated Fomin-Zelevinsky surface cluster algebra. Additionally, we establish a recursive formula for F-polynomials in the context of the Fomin-Zelevinsky finite type A cluster algebra. This formula is constructed using a recursive technique based on the Kac matrix and is derived from the combinatorics of F-polynomials in the associated F-PZ A cluster algebra.

FIDO2, a collaborative initiative by the Fast Identity Online (FIDO) Alliance and the Identity Access Management Alliance (IAMA), represents a significant advancement in authentication. It is a modern standard designed to supersede traditional password-based login methods, offering robust security against phishing and brute force attacks. This paper provides an overview of FIDO2, its underlying mechanisms, and its potential to enhance user experience. Additionally, we discuss the security and privacy advantages of this standard, its alignment with current regulatory compliance efforts, and its potential to foster a more secure digital future.

This study examines Weyl-Wigner calculus applied to lattice models, specifically addressing the Weyl symbol of the tight-binding Hamiltonian. It is demonstrated that this symbol can be expressed as a Fourier series with respect to the lattice basis, where the coefficients correspond to the Fourier transform of the Hamiltonian in real space. Furthermore, the corresponding Weyl-Wigner symbol for the corresponding evolution operator is analyzed. It is shown that this symbol exhibits periodicity in momentum space, mirroring the structure of the Brillouin zone, while maintaining anti-periodicity in imaginary time.

This study examines how the design of YouTube impacts users' perceived agency, defined as the ability to achieve goals and exert control within an online environment. Drawing on a survey of 1,000 YouTube users, the research reveals that platform design influences feelings of agency differently for creators versus viewers. YouTube's algorithmic curation is found to erode viewer agency by fostering passive consumption, whereas users perceive greater creator agency due to the platform's affordances for self-expression. Additionally, the research identifies demographic and usage patterns that correlate with these feelings of agency.

This study demonstrates that the $\pi$-calculus, when equipped with may-testing semantics, possesses both behaviourally complete and finitely executable characteristics, thereby resolving an ongoing open problem. Notably, our proof marks the first successful affirmation of behavioral completeness for the $\pi$-calculus. To achieve this, we propose a new, finite may-testing model for processes that is both sound and strictly a subset of may-testing while maintaining a perfect sound-and-complete correspondence with the $\pi$-calculus's may-testing congruence.

This study introduces a compact algorithm that seamlessly enumerates the space of ordered trees in constant time, not just from one to the next, but also generating them via a gray coding scheme where consecutive labels differ at a single leaf position. Central to these results are two combinatorial mappings grounded in the relationships between ordered trees and Dyck paths.

sPHENIX is a high-energy physics experiment at Brookhaven National Lab's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, designed to investigate the properties of strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma. It features a multi-layer tracking system with a vertex resolution of approximately 10 microns, enabling the study of heavy flavor hadrons and their decay products. To support sPHENIX's scientific goals, the ACTS software framework has been integrated to deliver a fast, high-precision track-finding algorithm. This system utilizes a hybrid approach combining deterministic and stochastic track seeding methods. The paper details the implementation of the ACTS software within the sPHENIX environment, evaluates its performance using Monte Carlo and real data, and outlines plans for its production use.

This study examines the numerical calculation of the jump term in the context of space-time finite elements for arbitrary temporal interpolation. The proposed methodology is applicable to various degrees of temporal smoothness and does not rely on a tensor-product structure. It utilizes a specific partitioning of the domain into two sub-regions to facilitate the computation. The paper demonstrates that this approach is efficient and can be adapted to different temporal approximation orders. Additionally, the authors establish theoretical bounds for the numerical error associated with the computed jump.

A signed graph is mono-directed when its edges are divided into two sets, one forming a directed graph and the other a oriented graph. This paper presents necessary and sufficient conditions for a mono-directed signed graph to admit a circular flow. As an immediate result, we also establish criteria for a oriented signed graph to possess a semi-flow.

The subset sum problem involves determining whether a specific target can be formed by summing a chosen collection of numbers from a given list. This work examines the deterministic version of the problem where the target is $t$ and the available numbers are $a_1, \dots, a_n$, operating under the constraint that $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \leq t$. We present a modular algorithm running in $O(t^{0.5399\dots})$ time to determine if $t$ can be expressed as $c_1a_1 + \dots + c_n a_n$ for integers $c_1, \dots, c_n$ satisfying $0 \leq c_i \leq m-1$, where $m$ is an integer modulus. This approach improves upon the prior $O(t^{0.6076\dots})$ bound established by Blömnstrand, Karpinska, and Vinzinc in 2021. Our methodology utilizes a divide-and-conquer strategy that splits the problem into two instances concerning $2^{1/2} \approx 0.63$ and $0.39$ of the original numbers, respectively.

Cell migration is a fundamental process in embryogenesis, yet the underlying mechanisms governing this movement remain unclear. In this study, we investigate the dynamics of hemocyte migration in Drosophila embryos, specifically examining how these cells navigate the embryo's dorsal surface. We demonstrate that these migrations follow a distinct pattern characterized by correlated movements between neighboring cells, a phenomenon we term "the anomalous tango." This behavior diverges from standard stochastic models of cell motility, which assume that each cell moves independently of its surroundings. Furthermore, we identify that this tango effect is driven by cell-cell adhesion, which facilitates the transfer of mechanical forces between cells. Consequently, our findings offer new insights into the mechanisms driving cell migration and highlight the significance of collective behaviors in this fundamental aspect of embryogenesis.

This study introduces a siamese network designed to enhance speech recognition through semi-supervised learning. The architecture comprises two parallel convolutional recurrent neural networks (ConvRNNs) that process input sequences independently, alongside a contrastive loss function applied to the output logit vectors to align similar samples and push apart dissimilar ones. This approach enables the model to learn robust feature representations for contrastive learning, facilitating the training of ConvRNNs to extract acoustic features that are discriminative for speech tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses a standard teacher model by 10% relative WER reduction on the LibriSpeech 1000 dataset when trained with only 10% labeled data, and achieves a 5% relative reduction on the full 1000-hour dataset with a label set of 500 hours.

This study examines the almost sure stabilization of adaptive linear-quadratic systems featuring a hidden Markov model, where the true state transition matrix belongs to a finite collection of valid options. The proposed methodology involves a novel algorithm that estimates the matrix by tracking the maximum likelihood of the observed state sequence. The research establishes that, under specific constraints, the closed-loop dynamics achieve almost sure exponential stability. These findings are substantiated by numerical experiments.

Active inference serves as a leading framework for modeling goal-directed behavior, with recent research demonstrating its efficacy in explaining cortical dynamics and predicting human actions. However, the model's current limitations stem from a reliance on a single modality and an inability to account for diverse behavioral drivers. This paper introduces a generalized active inference architecture capable of integrating multiple modalities and establishing goals based on temporal logic, temporal inference, and varying cost functions. We demonstrate that this design enables the model to perform multi-task learning, predict human conduct, and simulate behaviors such as the "streak effect" and goal-directed navigation. Furthermore, we illustrate how the model can dynamically shift attention between modalities and adapt its processing to novel environments.

This study examines the hydrodynamic framework of cold quark-gluon plasma (cQGP) to investigate the behavior of cold fluids within this environment. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, cQGP hydrodynamics yield the nonlinear, first-order, compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations, which are characterized by the presence of solitary wave solutions. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of these solitary waves and determine that they remain stable across a broad spectrum of parameters.

We establish that a k-space which is both locally metrizable and locally compact must be compact. Furthermore, we prove that a metrizable space is Eberlein-Grothendieck precisely when it is $\sigma$-compact. These findings offer a novel approach to addressing questions by Arhangel'skii and Valdivia.

The concept of isochronicity, which denotes a system possessing constant period behavior near a singular point, is a longstanding challenge in the theory of ordinary differential equations. This study presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing isochronicity in reversible systems with 1 degree of freedom. We demonstrate that, for reversible systems where the isochronicity condition holds, the vector field must be expressible as a specific linear combination of a Hamiltonian vector field and the gradient of the period function. This representation is pivotal for resolving the isochronicity problem, as it establishes a necessary condition for the potential, thereby enabling a more direct investigation into the problem.

This study introduces a novel method for constructing periodic orbits within the Lorenz system by leveraging similarity signature curves. The approach involves adjusting a single parameter in the vector field until the similarity curve exhibits self-intersection, marking the emergence of such an orbit. Utilizing numerical simulations, the authors demonstrate that this technique effectively identifies all known periodic orbits in the system, including those with arbitrary Poincaré maps. The method's practical utility is further highlighted by its application to control periodic orbits and to the task of parameter estimation.

This paper investigates the local absolute continuity property (LAN) for a general model involving an exponential process driven by a Lévy process. The mean and covariance structures of this model are derived from the drift and coefficients of the underlying stochastic differential equations (SDEs). We demonstrate that for a broad category of such SDEs, the resulting solutions generate Lévy-driven stochastic processes that exhibit LAN. Furthermore, the LAN for the specific case involving a standard Poisson process is examined in depth. Finally, the asymptotic behavior of the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for the parameters of a linear SDE with constant coefficients, as analyzed by the Heston model, is also discussed.

We introduce FNetAR, a new autoregressive framework that leverages global attention via Fourier transforms to model long-range dependencies in sequential data. This approach utilizes a unique tokenization scheme that groups consecutive tokens into fixed-size vectors, creating a compact sequence that encodes both local and global sequence details. Our findings demonstrate that FNetAR outperforms current autoregressive baselines, such as the autoregressive FNet, across various tasks including image modeling, language modeling, and DNA sequence prediction. Notably, FNetAR achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR100 and ImageNet-1K, surpassing autoregressive baselines by 1.5% and 0.6%, respectively. Additionally, FNetAR matches the performance of Transformer-XL on the Penn Treebank while requiring only 20% of its training time.

This study examines the cosmological evolution of Generalized Ghost Pilgrim Dark Energy (GGPDE) within Saez-Ballester's gravitational framework. The research investigates how the GGPDE energy density scale factor evolves over time, analyzing the resulting cosmic expansion and the corresponding age of the universe. The findings indicate that the Saez-Ballester theory, when applied to GGPDE, supports both decelerated and accelerated expansion phases depending on the chosen parameters. Furthermore, the derived expressions for cosmic age demonstrate that these specific models yield older ages than those predicted by the $\Lambda$CDM model.

This study examines a scenario where numerous users compete to establish virtual network functions (VNFs) within the context of mobile edge computing (MEC). Each user must select a specific set of VFNs to satisfy service requirements, while simultaneously choosing their data path and the location of the VFNs to provide these services. This interaction is modeled as a non-cooperative game where the objective is to maximize the sum of the users' utility and the service provider's profit. The paper first demonstrates the existence of a pure strategy Nash equilibrium (NE) and establishes that this equilibrium is also a maximum in terms of the game value. To address the computational challenges associated with finding the NE, we introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) approach. This method enables users to learn a strategy that approximates the NE by employing a Markov decision process (MDP) to represent the game environment. Furthermore, the paper investigates the scenario where users lack knowledge of the system's state, presenting a new MDP formulation that allows users to derive a strategy near the NE based solely on action history. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed reinforcement learning and learning-based strategies.

We examine a (1+1)-dimensional Dirac fermion model incorporating random masses, where the random mass term is characterized by a two-point correlation function that follows a power law. Utilizing a renormalization group approach, we identify the critical exponent of the mass disorder and the anomalous dimension of the random mass operator. Our findings indicate that the random mass operator is irrelevant, a result that aligns with previous numerical simulations.

We examine the strong isospin violation within the fundamental Sp(4) gauge theory by analyzing the mass spectrum of the lightest pseudscalar mesons. This work involves a combined approach using the lattice and continuum frameworks. We first present results from a lattice calculation employing the domain-wall fermion method, which demonstrates that the continuum limit can be achieved with a minimal number of lattice spacings. Subsequently, we utilize these data points to construct a continuum effective field theory, which subsequently facilitates the computation of the meson mass spectrum in the continuum regime.

We report on the structural, magnetic, and thermodynamic properties of Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$, a new member of the $A$NiTeO$_{6}$ family ($A$ = K, Rb, Cs, R$_3$). This material crystallizes in the monoclinic space group C2/c, featuring zigzag chains of Ni$^{2+}$ ions ($S$ = 1) separated by TeO$_{6}$ octahedra. Unlike its alkali variants with K, Rb, Cs, and R$_3$ cations, Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ exhibits a distinct magnetic ground state characterized by a zigzag spin arrangement. This configuration arises from competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, which are supported by inelastic neutron scattering data. Furthermore, we observe a spin-gap opening at low temperatures, attributed to the Na$_{4}$NiTeO$_{6}$-specific deficiency of $\delta$ Na ions.

Smart vehicular networks are increasingly vital for enhancing road safety and reducing traffic congestion, yet their deployment faces significant hurdles, primarily stemming from the need to establish trust among vehicles and infrastructure. This paper introduces a conceptual framework designed to facilitate reliable communication within smart vehicular environments by addressing the challenge of trust assignment. This framework integrates a dynamic trust model, a trust evaluation mechanism, and a trust storage component, all of which operate on a probabilistic basis to accommodate uncertainty. The study further examines the framework's specific attributes, including its adaptability, scalability, and capacity to manage both positive and negative information. Additionally, the paper outlines the framework's limitations and proposes avenues for future research.

This paper introduces a method for approximating functions that are both monotone and possess a strong gradient, utilizing a cubic spline interpolant defined on a non-uniform mesh. The mesh node spacing is adjusted to ensure the interpolant's derivative remains bounded within a specified limit. The analysis demonstrates that this cubic spline interpolant maintains a strong uniform convergence toward the underlying function, regardless of whether it is monotonic increasing or decreasing.

This study investigates exact Taub-NUT and scalar-hair black bounces within a framework of Einstein-Maxwell theory coupled to complex scalars in a $(d+1)$-dimensional Anti-de Sitter background. We derive the general form of these configurations for arbitrary dimensions, which are expressed as solutions to a single ordinary differential equation. We demonstrate that the black bounces exhibit a hair phase transition analogous to those found in previously studied real scalar theories. Furthermore, we establish that the $AdS$ Taub-NUT spacetime serves as a limiting case of the $AdS$ black bounces when their scalar charge vanishes.

This study introduces a specialized annotation tool designed to assist researchers in categorizing audio clips using extensive taxonomies. A primary hurdle in this domain is the cognitive burden of navigating large classification schemas, which can lead to errors or omissions. To address this, we developed a system that employs a retrieval-based methodology, utilizing retrieval scores to dynamically prioritize and adjust the size of the category list presented to annotators. Empirical results from categorizing 1,000 clips from the Urban Sound Dataset (containing 104 classes) demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances annotation speed and reduces the count of missed categories.

We introduce a novel approach to analyzing the dynamics of complex systems, which we term dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). This framework offers a comprehensive analytical description of the dynamics of a broad spectrum of systems, including ecosystems, reaction networks, and other similar models. By utilizing the theory, we derive a set of exact equations that govern the time evolution of the system's moments. This allows for a direct characterization of the system's dynamics, which can be further analyzed using established techniques. This work demonstrates the versatility of DMFT by applying it to various complex systems, including the Lotka-Volterra model, the replicator dynamics model, and the Lotka-Volterra-Smelnikov model.

We examine the distribution of avalanche sizes within a single site- and bond-induced Cayley tree model, demonstrating that it follows an exponential pattern. This outcome is established by deriving and solving an integral equation for the probability distribution.

The comprehension of discourse is a foundational element in human language understanding. While the significance of discourse comprehension has been acknowledged for decades, its role in answering questions is often overlooked. This paper posits that discourse comprehension serves as a vital prerequisite for addressing questions. To demonstrate this, we introduce a question-answering framework that explicitly models the inter-sentence connections found in discourse. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, the system identifies and categorizes the relationships between consecutive sentences; second, the system answers queries by synthesizing both local information within sentences and global context derived from these relations. We evaluated this approach on a dataset of questions requiring extensive local and global comprehension, achieving a 60% F1 score. These findings indicate that modeling sentence connections is essential for effectively addressing complex questions.

This review examines the application of the perfectly matched layer (PML) to hyperbolic wave equations, with particular attention to the numerical discretization of these systems. We begin by deriving the PML formulation for a general system of first-order hyperbolic equations, followed by a detailed analysis of the PML applied to the two-dimensional acoustic wave equation. This specific case is significant because it represents a standard model for acoustic waves in two dimensions, is frequently used to validate the PML, and can be transformed into a first-order system of equations. We then present the finite element discretization of the PML formulation for two-dimensional acoustic waves, contrasting it with the PML method for first-order hyperbolic systems. The review concludes by summarizing key findings and identifying open research questions.

This research investigates the deformation and fragmentation of droplets induced by laser pulses. The interaction between laser pulses and droplets was examined using a 1064-nm pulsed laser with a 100 fs duration, where the laser energy was regulated to control the pulse intensity. The resulting droplet dynamics were captured using a high-speed camera. The findings indicate that droplet deformation and subsequent fragmentation are governed by the pulse intensity, with a specific threshold intensity identified for initiating fragmentation. The study further analyzes the relationship between laser pulse energy and the resulting droplet fragments.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with billions of devices expected to be connected by 2025, a growth driven by the need for real-time data processing and the adoption of diverse IoT applications. However, the resulting IoT traffic is characterized by high volume, heterogeneity, and mobility, presenting significant challenges for network operators. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel IoT traffic orchestration framework that integrates Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub) mechanisms. This proposed framework offers a flexible architecture capable of handling heterogeneous IoT traffic efficiently. Furthermore, the authors introduce a Pub/Sub-based controller that manages traffic orchestration and an intelligent controller that utilizes machine learning to optimize traffic flow. Simulation results demonstrate that this framework significantly reduces end-to-end latency and improves the reliability of the IoT network.

The LkHα 330 protoplanetary disk, a young system (age ~1 Myr) located at 140 pc, exhibits a complex structure characterized by a prominent inner cavity in its millimeter-wave continuum emission. This study presents new ALMA observations of the disk, revealing a complex, multi-component architecture in its spectral energy distribution (SED) that spans from 0.3 to 1.3 mm. Analysis of the SED indicates that the millimeter-wave-emitting dust population is best modeled by a two-component fit: a compact inner disk component with a radius of 10.5 ± 1.0 au and a more extended outer disk component with a radius of 30.5 ± 1.0 au. The inner disk's spectral index of 2.1 ± 0.2 suggests a dust size distribution dominated by millimeter-sized grains, whereas the outer disk's spectral index of 3.5 ± 0.2 implies a population dominated by sub-millimeter-sized grains. Furthermore, the outer disk's inclination is measured at 10.5 ± 1.0 degrees, while the inner disk's inclination is 20.5 ± 1.0 degrees. These results suggest that the inner disk is a tilted structure situated within the cavity, while the outer disk represents the main disk material. This work introduces a novel distance metric for the space of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, designated as the vector-valued Fréchet-Dobesin distance. This study examines one-dimensional F_{q^2}-linear codes over F_{q^2} that are both additive and self-orthogonal under the trace-based Hermitian product. By introducing a novel class of codes known as F_q-linear conjugucyclic codes, we establish that they form a vector space over F_{q^2}. Furthermore, we determine the dimensionality of these codes, analyze their hierarchical lattice structure, and investigate their behavior under Hermitian duality. Additionally, we provide a classification of these codes for the specific case where q = 2.

This topical group aims to enhance the Community's understanding of the roles of Career Pipeline and Development (ComDF2) within the High Energy Physics (HEP) community. It seeks to identify ComF2's current status, pinpoint specific challenges, and outline opportunities for future contributions. The initiative involves three main deliverables: first, assessing the current state of ComF2 and its Community impact; second, detailing the specific challenges and opportunities ComDF2 encounters; and third, providing recommendations for the Community to address these issues. The final output will be a concise report summarizing these findings, intended to support Community committees and bodies in their planning and decision-making processes.

This study reports on the measurement of $W$ boson polarisation within top-antitop ($t\bar{t}$) decay events, utilizing proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector at CERN. The analysis focuses on the $t\bar{t}$ channel featuring a single isolated charged lepton and significant jet activity. The findings indicate that top quarks are produced with longitudinal polarization, a result consistent with the Standard Model's prediction of the top quark mass being significantly larger than the electroweak scale. The measured ratio of longitudinal to transverse $W$ boson polarisation is determined to be $0.66 \pm 0.08$ (statistical) $\pm 0.04$ (systematic). This value aligns with Standard Model expectations for a top quark mass of 173 GeV, which forecasts a ratio of 0.69, with a deviation of no more than 5 standard deviations.

This study revisits the light-cone distribution amplitude (LCDAs) of $D$ mesons, specifically focusing on the $D^0$ meson. We investigate the twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes, which are essential for analyzing rare radiative $B \to D \to PP$ decays involving pseudoscalar mesons. Utilizing QCD light-cone sum rules, we derive the first-ever QCD-predicted values for the twist-2, 3 LCDAs, including their respective first two moments. Furthermore, we examine the potential impact of parity violation on the twist-3 CDAs. Our findings indicate that the impact of these violations is negligible.

The power hypergraph $\mathcal{P}(G)$ of a graph $G$ is a multihypgraph where each vertex set $V_k(G)$ forms a hyperedge containing all $k$-tuples of vertices from $G$. This paper determines the spectrum of $\mathcal{P}(G)$ and establishes that the power hypergraph is acyclic if and only if the graph $G$ contains at most one edge. Additionally, we investigate signed subgraphs of $G$, defining their eigenvalues, and demonstrate that the largest eigenvalue of any signed subgraph $\mathcal{H}$ does not exceed the largest eigenvalue of $G$. We further prove that this largest eigenvalue equals $G$'s largest eigenvalue precisely when $\mathcal{H}$ is bipartite, provided $G$ is not bipartite.

This study derives analytical performance bounds for localisation within the constellation of Starlink satellites, utilizing the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) to establish limits on positioning accuracy. The analysis evaluates how various parameters influence these bounds, including the elevation of the target object, signal-to-noise ratio, orbital geometry, and the timing of localisation events. The resulting expressions are formulated as functions of these factors to facilitate a comprehensive assessment of potential performance.

We report the detection of transit timing variations (TTVs) in the hot Jupiter XO-3b, which manifest as a sinusoidal pattern with a 1.5-year period. This period aligns with the system's orbital period, indicating that the variations result from tidal evolution. Our analysis reveals that the observed TTVs are consistent with a tidal evolution model assuming a tidal quality factor of $\log_{10}(Q') = 4.7$ and a current orbital eccentricity of $e = 0.011$. This suggests that the planet's orbit is evolving from an eccentric state toward a circular configuration. We propose that the high eccentricity of XO-3b originated from a past planet-planet interaction, likely involving a now-missing companion.

The 21-cm global experiment faces a significant hurdle: the signal is extremely faint, often being obscured by system noise that is orders of magnitude stronger. To address this, the Noise Calibration (NoisyCal) technique was developed to extract the signal from system noise. This approach involves injecting a known noise level into the receiver and measuring its output to determine the gain, which is subsequently used to normalize the data. This process is repeated across various noise levels throughout the observation period. The NoisyCal method has been successfully applied to the EDGES and CHIME experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness. However, the current implementation relies on a fixed gain model, which may not accurately reflect the true receiver behavior. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for noise calibration that accounts for the uncertainty in the gain model. The method employs a Gaussian prior for the gain and utilizes Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to estimate the posterior distribution of the system noise. The results indicate that the Bayesian approach yields more precise noise estimates than the standard fixed-gain model. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the NoisyCal method can be adapted to scenarios involving non-linear gain characteristics.

This paper examines the genus $0$ equivariant Gromov-Witten theory of the projective bundle $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})$ over a base $B$, where $\mathcal{E}$ is a vector bundle on $B$. We introduce a novel closed formula for a generating series of equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants across arbitrary dimensions of $B$. This result relies on a new construction of a map connecting a novel equivariant K-theory object for $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})$ to the equivariant K-theory of $B$.

We establish prime number theorem estimates that remain valid for intervals of length $T^{1/2+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$, where the interval is denoted as $[x,x+x^{1+\epsilon}]$. These results extend the work of the current and their collaborators, who previously proved similar outcomes for intervals of length $T^{1/4+\epsilon}$ just prior to the preprint version of this study.

This study introduces a statistical model designed to analyze Alzheimer's disease clinical trials, specifically targeting the natural cubic spline fitting of the log-hazard ratio. By treating the log-hazard ratio as a smooth function of time, the approach offers a more precise estimate of treatment efficacy compared to standard methods that rely solely on hazard ratios. Additionally, the log-hazard ratio can be expressed as the sum of an overall mean effect and an individual effect derived from the spline. We demonstrate that this framework can be implemented using a generalized linear model with an interaction term between time and individual effects, where the coefficients for the spline are constrained to sum to zero.

This paper introduces a crowdsourcing algorithm designed to assist vehicles in locating available parking spaces. The proposed method utilizes a distributed architecture that leverages information shared by nearby vehicles to streamline navigation toward parking spots. The study presents a theoretical analysis of this algorithm, establishing that it guarantees the discovery of the nearest occupied spot in linear time relative to the total number of cars. Furthermore, simulations were conducted on a real-world map of the Greater Toronto Area to evaluate the proposed distributed parking solution. The results indicate that the algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods, reducing search time by approximately 50% and the total distance driven by 20%.

The effectiveness of flat minima optimizers in achieving better generalization has been extensively studied, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of these optimizers within the framework of kernel ridge regression. We demonstrate that flat minima optimizers function as spectral regularizers, with the specific form of regularization depending on the optimization algorithm employed. Our findings indicate that this spectral bias is fundamentally linked to the algorithm's memory capacity. Furthermore, we establish that the generalization performance of these optimizers is governed by the alignment between the regularized solution and the target function's representation in the tangent kernel space. Finally, the proposed theoretical results are validated through experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel SEIRS epidemic model for COVID-19, grounded in the hypothesis that acquired immunity is negligible. This framework is derived by applying a specific simplification to a broader class of SEIRS models. The research demonstrates that the model's dynamics are governed by two critical parameters: the basic reproduction number, $R_0$, and the rate of loss of immunity. The authors establish that, under the identified extreme condition, the epidemic's outcome is entirely dictated by these two factors. Furthermore, the paper examines the influence of various interventions on the disease's trajectory. The findings indicate that while lockdowns and social distancing are essential for epidemic control, their effectiveness is contingent upon these two parameters. The study concludes by analyzing the implications of these results for the current pandemic situation.

Word embeddings have become a cornerstone of natural language processing, with numerous variants developed to optimize performance across different tasks. Despite this, a standardized method for selecting the most appropriate variant for a specific application remains absent. This study presents a novel framework designed to evaluate and choose between diverse embedding types. We introduce a new metric that quantifies the contextual performance of an embedding within a specific model and application, thereby enabling the selection of a single best-fit variant. This metric relies on a set of heuristics that assess the quality of a word's context, including its size, the semantic diversity of neighboring words, and the uniformity of their distribution. We validate this selection process using multiple models and applications, demonstrating that it effectively identifies the highest-performing variant. Additionally, we explore how the framework can guide the design of future embedding models.

This study investigates the characteristics of cliques within high-density random geometric graphs, defined by a node density parameter $\lambda$ that approaches infinity. We examine scenarios where the cluster radius $r$ scales as $r = \alpha n^{-1/d}$. Specifically, we demonstrate that for $\alpha < \alpha_c(d)$, the largest $k$-clique has size $(1-o(1))\lambda r^d$ with high probability, whereas for $\alpha > \alpha_c(d)$, its size grows superlinearly relative to $\lambda r^d$. Furthermore, we establish that the number of such cliques is asymptotically Poisson distributed. These findings extend previous research by Bhamidi, van Ryzin, and Van Handel, who addressed the maximum clique size, as well as works by Dey, Gao, and Mukherjee and by Dey and Gao regarding the number of cliques.

We introduce an innovative method for modeling self-gravitating fluids in a rotating state, rooted in the Lagrangian framework. This approach utilizes the Lagrangian displacement to formulate variations in the gravitational potential and the specific internal energy. By incorporating these adjustments into the variational principle, we derive the Euler equation and the Poisson equation. This new Lagrangian formulation is mathematically equivalent to the conventional Euler equation expressed in Eulerian variables alongside the standard Poisson equation. We demonstrate the procedure by deriving a rotating star solution, which is then compared with a comparable result obtained through a standard Eulerian analysis.

This study investigates the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) spacetime within the framework of Palatini $f(R)$ gravity, treating both the matter and the connection as completely independent. Under the condition of zero pressure, the derived field equations are expressed in terms of the Ricci tensor, yielding a modified version of the original LTB metric. This modified metric is then employed to examine the universe's expansion history. Furthermore, the study analyzes the cosmic acceleration history, concluding that the expansion history is independent of the function $f(R)$, whereas the acceleration history exhibits a dependence on it.

We demonstrate that any $N$-partite quantum state with a Schmidt rank exceeding $N$ exhibits strong quantum nonlocality, defined as the capability to block any local measurement from detecting non-classical correlations if one party performs a specific action. This finding extends our earlier work on bipartite systems, which revealed that bipartite states with Schmidt rank 2 are locally indistinguishable from classical states accessible via local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Our results confirm that both LOCC and separable operations fail to access these "nonlocal in any local measurement" states, thereby establishing a robust form of quantum nonlocality for such systems.

This paper introduces a novel reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) designed for transmissive applications, marking the first demonstration of such a device. The prototype, measuring 1.25λ × 1.25λ, integrates 16 unit cells, each utilizing a varactor diode to enable two distinct transmission states. The study validates the device's performance through both experimental results and simulations, specifically examining how the transmitted signal strength varies with the phase shift of individual elements. The authors further analyze the efficacy of this transmissive RIS in a 6G context, comparing its advantages against reflective and refractive counterparts. The analysis highlights that transmissive RIS offers superior link gain and enhanced coverage, particularly in scenarios with high reflection coefficients. Finally, the paper outlines a practical architecture for a RIS controller capable of managing phase shifts across all elements and evaluates the system's overall performance.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) represents a rapidly evolving area in RL, where the objective is to derive an optimal policy from static datasets without further interaction with the environment. While recent research has primarily concentrated on function approximation within offline RL, the linear function class remains a foundational benchmark for evaluating theoretical guarantees. This paper investigates the linear function class under a novel framework that integrates linear RL with linear programming. By examining this hybrid framework, we derive a regret bound for offline RL that is nearly optimal, matching the performance gap of online RL up to logarithmic factors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the linear programming framework is capable of achieving near-optimal results for online RL.

This note outlines the construction of free $A_\infty$-categories and natural transformations between them, which are defined as higher homotopy cocategories. We demonstrate that these structures arise via the Dold-Kan correspondence, linking them to the theory of higher groupoids. Furthermore, the work examines connections with the theory of $A_\infty$-categories developed by Ginzburg, Manin, and Schiro-Manso.

This paper examines planar three-body systems where the masses are constant, focusing on the behavior of solutions to Newton's equations. It is demonstrated that for any such configuration, the set of times at which the bodies align into a straight line forms a closed set. Furthermore, for any given $T>0$, the specific intervals within $[0,T]$ during which these alignments occur can be precisely determined. The analysis also addresses the nature of these intervals when they are not contiguous, revealing that the durations of the gaps between them are bounded from below by a constant strictly greater than zero.

Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) is a powerful technique for investigating the microenvironment of fluorophores, including variations in pH, temperature, and ionic strength. This study introduces a deconvolution method to enhance the resolution of FLIM images, thereby improving the precision of lifetime measurements. The approach involves convolving the fluorescence lifetime images with a point spread function (PSF) to generate a model of the expected data, followed by an iterative refinement of the PSF to minimize the discrepancy between this model and the original FLIM images. The effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through the analysis of a confocal FLIM dataset of a two-component sample.

This study introduces a novel approach to modeling user behavior for personalized product search, leveraging graph neural networks to capture both global and local patterns within the user-product interaction network. The core methodology involves constructing a graph where nodes represent individual users and items, with edges signifying interactions. We then develop a graph convolutional network (GCN) to aggregate neighborhood information for each node, effectively synthesizing both global and local structural data. This process generates comprehensive user and product embeddings that facilitate the prediction of future interactions. Experimental validation on the Alibaba Taobao dataset demonstrates that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both click-through rate (CTR) prediction and next-item recommendation.

Recent years have seen manifold learning attract significant interest from researchers due to its ability to extract deep, low-dimensional representations from high-dimensional data. However, most existing approaches rely on labeled data, which is often unavailable in real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised deep manifold learning method that utilizes both labeled and unlabeled data. Specifically, we employ a deep autoencoder to capture the underlying manifold structure and develop a new loss function designed to preserve local neighborhood relationships. We further incorporate a graph regularization term to strengthen the consistency of the learned representations. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm (GA) designed to design non-orthogonal sequences for grant-free massive machine-type communications. The method optimizes sequence correlation properties by addressing two challenges: the discrete nature of the search space and the high dimensionality of the problem. The first stage utilizes a binary encoding scheme to identify the optimal set of non-zero entries, while the second stage employs a real-valued encoding scheme to determine the optimal values of those entries. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) method in terms of the number of successfully decoded packets.

This represents a significant improvement over the previous best result, which achieved only $k = \Theta(N^{1/4})$. This study introduces a novel regularization technique designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks. By leveraging the concept of invariance, the method incorporates transformations into the loss function to ensure that transformed versions of an input yield identical predictions as the original. This approach is versatile, applicable to various classification tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and action recognition. We demonstrate the technique's efficacy through experiments on the ImageNet dataset, the Cityscapes dataset, and the KITTI dataset, where it achieves substantial improvements in generalization performance.

This study examines the potential of future muon colliders for discovering and investigating axion-like particles (ALPs). We establish a framework for the production and detection of these particles at high-energy muon colliders, detailing their implications for both single-pass and circular collider designs. By analyzing the potential for detecting ALPs through the "muon pair portal," we determine the sensitivity reach for both single and circular collider scenarios. We also examine the potential for detecting ALPs through the "lepton pair portal," which is particularly advantageous for identifying low-mass ALPs. Finally, we evaluate the potential for detecting displaced muon pairs and ALPs decaying into displaced lepton pairs, which is especially effective for identifying long-lived ALPs.

Modern data-centric workloads, such as machine learning, rely on metadata to function effectively. Metadata systems (MetaDatabases) store this information, yet they are frequently underutilized. Although numerous cross-layer optimizations exist for data-centric systems, they are typically implemented directly within the underlying storage engine, which hinders their reusability and limits applicability across different systems. To address this, we introduce MetaSys, a practical open-source metadata management system designed to enable and assess cross-layer optimizations. MetaSys offers three key capabilities: (1) a modular architecture that supports flexible implementation and evaluation of optimizations; (2) interfaces connecting to various data engines, allowing it to serve as a drop-in replacement for metadata management in diverse data-centric systems; and (3) a framework for building and testing novel optimizations. We demonstrate MetaSys's utility by implementing and evaluating two optimizations: a query optimizer and a caching strategy. Experimental results indicate that MetaSys delivers significant performance improvements, with query execution times reduced by up to 1.5x and query response times reduced by up to 1.5x, depending on the specific data engine used.

This paper introduces transfer learning strategies for image classification, leveraging pre-trained models on existing datasets to enhance performance on target data. We introduce two specific approaches: the first employs a Siamese network to learn from pairwise image relationships within the target dataset, while the second utilizes synthetic data generated through image warping. Our results demonstrate that our techniques achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art models, with the Siamean network variant specifically excelling on the Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-100 challenges.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have proven highly effective for sequential data tasks, yet they often struggle with capturing long-term dependencies due to vanishing gradients. This paper introduces Fourier Recurrent Units (FRUs), a novel architecture designed to overcome these limitations. By utilizing Fourier series, FRUs can theoretically model dependencies across arbitrarily long time scales. We provide a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that FRUs can theoretically achieve convergence to the optimal solution for tasks involving long-term dependencies. Furthermore, we present a new loss function tailored to enhance the training of FRUs for capturing long-range relationships. Experimental results on standard benchmarks substantiate the theoretical findings, confirming that FRUs excel at learning long-term dependencies.

This study examines the problem of identifying an optimal policy within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) that is defined by a known transition matrix but an uncertain reward matrix. We introduce a sequential procedure that alternates between gathering data and refining estimates of the reward matrix, aiming to determine the best policy with a pre-specified level of confidence. We establish an upper limit on the number of required samples, which scales linearly with the total count of transitions needed to discover an optimal policy in an MDP with a fully known reward matrix. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for MDPs where the reward structure is fixed but unknown, demonstrating that our proposed upper bound matches this lower bound up to multiplicative factors determined solely by the MDP's topology.

We introduce a novel method for creating high-intensity, circularly polarized attosecond electron bunches utilizing dual-wake injection. This approach employs a laser pulse with circular polarization to generate the initial transverse field, followed by a second transverse laser pulse to induce scattering within a plasma medium. This scattering mechanism effectively separates the scattered electrons from the main plasma background. The resulting electron bunch exhibits intensities orders of magnitude higher than those achievable with conventional methods, while maintaining polarization. Furthermore, the technique offers a highly flexible approach to tuning the bunch's energy and spatial distribution.

This study explores the emergence of complexity in astrophysical systems, ranging from stars to life. It begins by examining how stellar populations evolve toward greater complexity, noting that while star formation is a chaotic process, the resulting systems display a consistent, orderly progression. This pattern is explained by the fact that stellar populations are not random collections of individual stars but are instead composed of systems that share a common evolutionary history. The paper then investigates the conditions necessary for life to arise, emphasizing that living organisms are not merely static entities but undergo a continuous trajectory of increasing complexity, characterized by a steady rise in the number of functional components and their interconnectivity. This perspective is supported by empirical data from both living and extinct biological populations. Finally, the text outlines a fundamental principle of astrophysical evolution: the evolution of complexity is a universal phenomenon that occurs across all scales of the universe, from subatomic particles to galaxies, and is driven by the drive to maximize entropy.

Research mapping relies on extensive repositories of publications and citations, which are frequently provided through AI-based tools. In this study, we examine how artificial intelligence can be employed to analyze climate change research, specifically by leveraging the free, open-source re3data database to identify relevant repositories. We selected the Grasp AI platform, an open-source solution, to evaluate re3data's list of data sources for generating research maps. Our analysis demonstrates that these AI-driven mapping tools offer significant advantages in terms of cost-efficiency and speed, making them ideal for creating rapid, exploratory analyses for policy and research planning. However, we also note that while the re3data database effectively catalogs scientific outputs, it may overlook grey literature, such as government reports. Consequently, we advise that when using such mapping services, it is essential to supplement automated data with manual curation to ensure the inclusion of critical non-peer-reviewed materials.

Android, the world's most widely adopted mobile operating system, is frequently targeted by adversaries seeking to compromise its security. A significant portion of these attacks exploits side-channel leaks inherent in the NDK, which are often introduced by developers due to poor coding practices. This paper introduces ASVAAN, a semi-automatic tool designed to identify side-channel vulnerabilities in NDK-based Android applications. ASVAAN operates in two phases: first, it automatically generates test cases to trigger the leaks, and second, it analyzes runtime data to pinpoint instances of side-channel exposure. We evaluated ASVAAN on a collection of 20 NDK applications, successfully detecting 12 vulnerabilities that remained undetected by prior methods.

Blockchain technology has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly for its role in facilitating secure, decentralized, and transparent transactions. Ethereum, a prominent blockchain platform, serves as a hub for decentralized applications (dApps) and smart contracts, enabling users to execute, monitor, and verify transactions. This study analyzes Ethereum's transaction graph by constructing and examining its ego networks. Specifically, we evaluate the structural and topological characteristics of these networks across various transaction labels. Our findings indicate that the network's structural properties are consistent regardless of the specific label applied. However, the nature of the labels significantly influences the degree distribution and the statistical properties of the degree distribution.

We report on the observation of quantum oscillations in a two-dimensional electron system (2DES) at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface under optical excitation. By analyzing the temperature dependence of the 2DES conductivity, we identify the oscillations, which exhibit a period corresponding to a magnetic field of 10 T. These features are attributed to the modulation of the 2DES carrier density by the incident light. We also observe that the magnitude of the conductivity oscillations increases with the laser power, a trend consistent with the observed rise in the 2DES's Hall mobility under illumination.

This research examines the inherent complexity of cut-elimination within the context of elementary multiplicative-additive linear logic (MLAL) and pomposity logic (PV). We demonstrate that the number of distinct cut-elimination steps required for a specific proof is constrained by a constant factor relative to the proof's size, a result that holds true for both logical systems. This finding represents the inaugural instance where such a constant-factor upper bound has been established for cut-elimination procedures in both MLAL and pomposity logic.

The Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra represents a deformation of the Heisenberg algebra defined by a parameter $\varepsilon$. When $\varepsilon$ is set to 0, this algebra simplifies to the Heisenberg algebra. We demonstrate that a pentagon identity holds within this Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra, thereby extending a previously established proof.

We introduce a novel photometric redshift algorithm, which utilizes data from the 4MOST-LSF survey covering the W-CDF-S and ELAIS-S1 regions. This method relies on the 0.36–4.5 micron spectral range, derived from the VLT/VIMOS instrument and the SDSS/UKIDSS surveys, respectively. The algorithm is designed to handle "forced photometry," meaning it incorporates data from the upcoming 4MOST-LSF survey even when specific source detections are absent. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using a simulated dataset, where it achieves a median redshift error of 0.014 and a normalized redshift scatter of 0.033. The algorithm's ability to handle missing detections is also assessed, revealing that the photometric redshift error increases by 0.006 when the detection is absent.

This study introduces a Bayesian decision support system designed to evaluate the viability of energy systems projects. It integrates a suite of Bayesian network models that represent the interplay between project characteristics, environmental factors, and financial metrics. By employing Bayesian network planning, the system calculates the probability of a project's success, enabling project managers to assess risks and make informed decisions regarding investment. The framework is designed to be flexible, allowing for the incorporation of new variables and the refinement of probability estimates as additional data emerges. The paper outlines the methodology for constructing these networks and validates the approach using a case study focused on wind energy systems.

The electronic wavefunction is characterized by a vast number of variables, yet it exhibits high structural sparsity. This work demonstrates that the two-electron wavefunction adheres to matrix product states (MPS) with a bond dimension of Three. This constraint holds regardless of the chosen spatial basis and remains valid for both spin-singlet and spin-singlet states. The study further establishes that wavefunctions derived from a specific class of highly entangled matrix product uniform states (MUPS) with a bond dimension of Infinity can be compressed into a two-electron wavefunction. This compression is achieved via a matrix-valued integral kernel, a concept closely related to the two-electron reduced density matrix (2-RDM).

We investigate a non-abelian dark matter framework featuring a vector dark matter candidate that interacts with the Standard Model via a heavy messenger sector. This sector includes a triplet of fermions and scalars that couple to the dark matter and generate contributions to both the muon and electron $g-2$ anomalies. We analyze the phenomenology of this model across direct detection experiments, collider searches, and lepton flavor violation measurements, identifying a viable parameter space that simultaneously explains the observed excesses in both muon and electron $g-2$.

The Digital Twin Earth (DTE) initiative seeks to create a dynamic, real-time digital representation of the planet to enhance decision-making and support human activities. A critical component of this initiative is the DTE Coasts project, which aims to deliver physics-based, real-time digital models of coastal flooding. A significant hurdle in this domain is the computational expense of existing hydrodynamic models, which are essential for forecasting flood events. To address this, we introduce a surrogate model utilizing neural operators to approximate the solution operator of the shallow water equations (SWEs). This approach offers a substantial speedup over traditional methods while maintaining high accuracy. We evaluated the surrogate model's performance using a dataset comprising 1000 simulations of the 2013 Hurricane Isaac event, covering the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Results indicate that the model accurately predicts flooding across the entire domain, with a maximum error of 0.2 meters in the Gulf of Mexico and 0.1 meters in the Atlantic Ocean.

The BeyondPlanck initiative, a collaborative effort among multiple institutions, aims to create a unified, open repository for all publicly available cosmological maps. This initiative is driven by the need to address critical challenges in reproducibility and ensuring the long-term accessibility of these datasets. As part of this work, Cosmoglobes—a web-based platform for visualizing and analyzing these maps—is being developed alongside the repository. This document outlines the project's objectives, details the current status of its development, and highlights the collaborative efforts of the BeyondPlanck team.

Reaction-diffusion Turing patterns are commonly observed in biological contexts, yet their investigation in spatially extended systems remains limited. This study examines the emergence of such patterns in a coupled network of reaction-diffusion systems, where diffusion occurs between nodes via a graph and information transmission is governed by a finite propagation model. We demonstrate that finite propagation significantly alters pattern formation, specifically enabling the creation of localized structures. Furthermore, we explore the system's dynamics in terms of its stability, its connection to the underlying graph's properties, and the influence of varying diffusion strength.

This paper demonstrates that Yang-Mills theory can be formulated in a quasiclassical manner by deriving a quasiclassical limit of the Dirac bracket for the Yang-Mills phase space. This approach yields a phase space that is both time-independent and position-dependent, characterized by the presence of Yang-Mills holonomies. Consequently, the quantum mechanical wave function transforms into a scalar defined on this modified phase space, while the Hamiltonian acquires a dependence on the Yang-Mills holonomy. To validate this framework, the study examines the $SU(2)$ Yang-Mills monopole, analyzing the Hamiltonian resulting from the trace of the holonomies. The analysis reveals that the Hamiltonian is a function of the radial coordinate, thereby confirming the consistency of the quasiclassical limit of Yang-Mills theory.

We present experimental findings on the polarization characteristics of single, self-assembled GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wires. These structures, created via Stranski-Krastanov growth, possess a wurtzite crystal structure and measure approximately 10 nm in width and 30 nm in length. The wires are positioned on a GaAs substrate with a 1.5 μm gap between them and are individually identified using photoluminescence microscopy. Our results indicate that the polarization dependence of the zero-phonon line (ZPL) emission varies with the wire's orientation relative to the excitation polarization. Specifically, the polarization anisotropy of the zero-phonon line exhibits a cos²θ relationship, where θ represents the angle between the detection polarization and the wire axis. This behavior is attributed to the anisotropic spatial confinement of the hole wavefunction within the wire. Additionally, we observe a significant polarization anisotropy in the emission of longitudinal optical (LO) phonons, which we explain through the anisotropic screening of the electron-hole Coulomb interaction by the surrounding dielectric material.

Opponent modeling is essential for achieving high performance in negotiation systems, yet it is constrained by the scarcity of data regarding specific opponent strategies. This paper introduces an opponent modeling framework for negotiation dialogues that leverages related data adaptation. The methodology involves three main steps: first, identifying and selecting dialogue data that are similar to the target opponent; second, training a model using these related datasets; and third, refining the model by fine-tuning it with limited dialogue data from the target opponent. Experiments conducted on the IACR Open Negotiation Dataset demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on the target opponent's data or on datasets from unrelated opponents.

Sequential experiments are gaining significant attention in both scientific research and industry. A primary challenge in this field is balancing the assignment of experimental units to treatment arms, a difficulty that becomes particularly pronounced when the number of units is limited and the number of treatment arms is large. To address this, we introduce a novel concept called the pigeonhole design. In this framework, each experimental unit is modeled as a vector, and the unit is assigned to the treatment arm that results in the smallest $l_1$ norm distance from that unit to the average of all previous units assigned to that specific treatment arm. We demonstrate that this design effectively balances assignments across all arms, offering a superior guarantee compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we illustrate how the pigeonhole design can be adapted for the adaptive randomization required in multi-armed bandit problems.

The interface between silicon and aluminum oxide (Al2O3) is critical for the reliability of power semiconductors, yet its chemical characteristics remain poorly understood. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the atomic-level bonding between Si and Al2O3. We demonstrate that the interfacial Al atoms form covalent bonds with Si, characterized by a 33% 2p character in the bonding states, indicating that the boundary is not ionic as previously assumed. Furthermore, the structural stability of the interface is maintained by the strong covalent nature of these bonds, which allows for the accommodation of the lattice mismatch between the two materials.

This study offers a meta-analysis of anomaly detection methods designed for streaming data, addressing the challenge of identifying irregularities in real-time. These methods face unique hurdles, such as the necessity to detect anomalies instantly, handle high-dimensional data, and adapt to evolving data distributions. Consequently, the authors developed a novel framework to categorize and evaluate existing approaches based on how they address these specific issues. This taxonomy facilitates the comparison of methods within and across categories, enabling users to select algorithms tailored to their particular application needs.

This study introduces a new approach for segmenting gliomas in brain MRI images by leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) paired with straightforward post-processing methods. The network architecture is designed to minimize computational requirements, ensuring it can be efficiently trained on standard hardware. The model utilizes three input channels: the original MRI scan, a gradient map, and a Laplacian image. The segmentation workflow involves a forward pass to generate a probability map, followed by a simplified algorithm that calculates the centroid of the largest connected component within this map. The training dataset consists of 100 annotated brain MRI images, comprising 50 cases of glioma tumors and 50 controls. The results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.815.

We introduce a theoretical framework for magnon-triplon scattering in antiferromagnets, wherein a triplon traveling along one crystallographic direction transitions into one or more triplons moving in a different direction. This scattering mechanism facilitates the generation of steady triplon currents, potentially enhancing the output of such currents in ferromagnets when coupled with an adjacent antiferromagnet.

This study introduces a novel numerical framework utilizing both $D_1G_1$ and $D_3G_1$ finite elements to address the 1-dimensional Rosenau equation. The analysis establishes the well-posedness of the problem and derives error bounds of order $O(h^{\min\{k+1,2\}})$ in the $L^2$ norm and $O(h^{\min\{k+1,\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\}})$ in the $H^1$ norm. Numerical experiments are subsequently performed to validate these theoretical findings.

This study investigates the stability of a coupled PDE framework comprising a linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system in the bulk and the nonlinear Euler equations for a fluid interface, utilizing the Caginalp--Mifflin formulation. By applying the compressibility constraint to derive a coupled evolution system, we establish conditions for weak solutions and their uniqueness, along with regularity estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework maintains weak solution stability upon discretization, thereby ensuring numerical well-posedness.

We present a theoretical investigation into the magnetic-field-driven Wigner crystallization of charged interlayer excitons within van der Waals heterostructures. By examining the interplay between magnetic fields and Coulomb interactions, we demonstrate that the localization of these excitons in the high-field regime is governed by a transition from delocalized to localized states. This transition is defined by a critical magnetic field, $B_c$, which is determined by the ratio of the Coulomb interaction strength to the magnetic length. We derive an analytical expression for $B_c$ and contrast it with numerical results, revealing that the transition is marked by a divergence in the exciton's magnetic moment. Furthermore, we analyze the system's phase diagram and identify a distinct region where interlayer excitons crystallize into a triangular lattice.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) has recently released a catalog containing 1.1 million medium-resolution stellar spectra, offering a powerful tool for studying stellar populations. However, the radial velocity (RV) data within this catalog currently lacks relative calibration, resulting in systematic offsets that hinder its utility for precise measurements. This study introduces a relative calibration method for LAMOST RVs by leveraging the precise RVs of 1,000 stars from Gaia DR3, which were cross-matched with the LAMOST catalog. A quadratic polynomial was fitted to the RV differences between the two catalogs to derive the necessary corrections. The findings indicate that the mean RV offset is 0.01 km s$^{-1}$, with a standard deviation of 0.12 km s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, the RVs exhibit a slight linear trend of 0.0004 km s$^{-1}$ per Ångström across the observed range of 3,700 to 5,200 Å. This linear trend correlates with the wavelength-dependent variations in the signal-to-noise ratio of the LAMOST spectra. Consequently, the proposed correction scheme effectively mitigates RV offsets in LAMOST medium-resolution spectra, thereby enhancing their accuracy for astrophysical investigations.

This study addresses the inverse scattering problem by determining an object's shape from its far-field pattern across various frequencies. We introduce a novel, fully automatic approach that utilizes deep neural networks to recover object shapes from measured scattering data. The methodology is built upon two key components: an axisymmetric equivariant neural network designed to model the unknown object, and a physics-informed loss function that leverages the wide-band Born approximation. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments involving prolate spheroids and a human head.

Accelerated degradation testing (ADT) is a prevalent methodology for forecasting product reliability and lifespan. Gamma processes are frequently employed to model degradation trajectories, while stress acceleration factors are often treated as uncertain parameters. This study introduces a novel Bayesian framework for estimating these stress acceleration factors when they exhibit uncertainty as random variables. The proposed model accommodates scenarios where two stress acceleration factors are stochastic and display mutual dependence. Bayesian inference is conducted using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to derive posterior distributions for the factors and associated hyperparameters. Furthermore, the framework predicts the time-to-failure for units subjected to specific stress levels. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study involving the estimation of time-to-failure for two-fraction bivariate gamma processes with dependent components, utilizing data from a novel ADT experiment.

We investigate the triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 200$ GeV using a multiphase transport model. The initial $v_3$ is calculated via the event-by-event Glauber model, while the final state evolution is simulated through a transport approach. The results indicate that the generated $v_3$ is predominantly determined by the initial spatial anisotropy and remains insensitive to the initial entropy density.

This study investigates the polytropic behavior of solar wind plasma within interaction regions formed between Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejections (ICMEs) and High-speed Streams (HSS). By analyzing data from the Advanced Composition and Particle detector (ACE) and the Wind spacecraft, we examine the plasma's polytropic index (γ) in these regions. Our findings indicate that ICME-HSS interaction regions exhibit a polytropic index (γ) of approximately 1.1, a value significantly lower than the γ ≈ 1.25 observed in both HSS and ICME regions independently. This discrepancy suggests that ICME-HSS interaction regions are more isothermal compared to individual ICMEs and HSS streams. Furthermore, we observed that the polytropic index (γ) in these interaction regions varies with the plasma's beta value, implying that the interaction between ICMEs and HSS alters the thermodynamic state of the solar wind plasma.

This paper examines the random waypoint (RWP) model, a widely adopted simulation framework for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). We derive the fundamental statistical properties of the RWP model, including distributions for path length, travel duration, and speed. Furthermore, we establish the model's ergodicity and demonstrate that the RWP model is a non-homogeneous Markov process. Additionally, we analyze velocity distributions for specific parameter sets, revealing that while the velocity distribution is not normally distributed, it closely resembles a Gamma distribution.

The microscopic collective inertial mass, a core component of the moment of inertia, is a critical element for calculating reaction cross-sections in the nuclear transfer domain. This mass is derived from the quasiparticle effective mass and the reduced mass of the reacting nuclei. Our analysis reveals that the nucleonic effective mass, which is pivotal for determining the quasiparticle effective mass, significantly influences the inertial mass in heavy-ion collisions. Specifically, when the nucleonic effective mass is low, the collective inertial mass is substantially reduced, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the suppression of the nucleonic effective mass. This finding offers new insights into the nuclear reaction mechanism, particularly regarding the collective inertial mass, providing fresh perspectives for theoretical investigations.

This study examines the regularity properties of solutions to conservation laws featuring discontinuous flux, specifically focusing on how singularities manifest at discontinuities. We introduce a fractional regularity result, establishing that near a singular point, the $L^\infty$ norm of the solution exhibits a fractional Sobolev regularity of order $1/2 - \delta$, where $\delta > 0$. This finding extends prior work by Bressan, Carrillo, Garavello, and Zambotti, who demonstrated that the solution possesses weak* $L^\infty$ regularity away from the singular set. Additionally, we provide an example indicating that weak* $L^\infty$ regularity does not hold in the $p$-space for any $p > 1$, away from the singular set.

This study introduces a novel Cell-Free Massive MIMO (CFmMIMO) architecture leveraging multi-carrier division duplex (MCDD) technology. By utilizing separate frequency bands for uplink and downlink transmissions, the system effectively mitigates radio frequency interference (RFI) and reduces the need for complex coordinated processing among distributed access points (APs). The research evaluates the system's performance through the derivation of the asymptotic downlink and uplink spectral efficiency (DL/UL SE) under various channel conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that the DL/UL SE performance of CFmMIMO with MCDD closely matches that of traditional massive MIMO systems employing time-division duplex (TDD) protocols.

The shuffle model of differential privacy offers a robust framework for privacy-preserving data analysis, where individual queries are anonymized by a shuffled server. This paper establishes tight lower and upper bounds for privacy loss across a broad class of query functions within this model. Specifically, we prove that for any query mechanism, a set of $n$ users, and a query function $f$, the total privacy loss does not exceed $n \cdot \Delta$, where $\Delta$ represents the query's sensitivity. We further demonstrate that accounting for the privacy loss of all aggregate functions involving $n$ users and up to $k$ queries is bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{k} \cdot \Delta)$. Consequently, our findings confirm that the privacy loss in the shuffle model scales with the square root of the number of queries, rather than linearly.

Orthogonal Time Frequency SEquential Multiplexing (OTFS) is a delay-Doppler domain modulation technique that has garnered significant attention for its robustness against high-mobility channels. However, current OTFS receivers rely on complex, computationally intensive algorithms, which hinders practical implementation. This paper introduces a low-complexity sequential receiver for OTFS systems. Initially, we propose a sequential minimum mean square error (MMSE) receiver that utilizes Doppler domain properties to derive a closed-form expression for the MMSE estimate of transmitted symbols. Subsequently, we develop a sequential minimum squared error (SMSE) receiver that leverages the proposed sequential MMSE output to generate an even lower-complexity solution. Simulation results demonstrate that both the SMSE and sequential MMSE receivers achieve performance comparable to the conventional OTFS receiver while offering significantly reduced computational complexity.
